title: Human Rights Challenges Today
subtitle: Narrativ versjon
description: A story about the new pressures testing human rights in our century -- climate change, digital surveillance, displacement and authoritarianism -- and how the framework must adapt.
competenceGoals: analyze contemporary global challenges through a human rights lens
discuss the relationship between climate change, migration, and human rights
evaluate how digital technology and authoritarianism threaten and can strengthen human rights protection

content.content:
## Old rights, new dangers

In many ways, the human rights project has been a quiet triumph. Slavery is now universally condemned, democracy has reached more countries than ever, literacy has soared and extreme poverty has fallen dramatically. And yet the twenty-first century is throwing up challenges that the framers of the Universal Declaration could barely have imagined.

Climate change threatens the basic rights to life, food, water and shelter for billions. Digital technology enables surveillance on a scale never before possible. The global refugee crisis has displaced over a hundred million people. Authoritarian governments are rolling back freedoms in many parts of the world. And stubborn inequalities of gender, race and wealth still deny full rights to vast numbers of people. The question this chapter asks is not whether the human rights framework still matters, but how it must adapt to meet dangers its authors never foresaw.

## When the climate threatens your rights

It may seem strange at first to call climate change a *human rights* issue, but the connection is direct. Rising temperatures, extreme weather, sea-level rise and resource scarcity threaten a whole range of fundamental rights. The *right to life* is endangered by deadly heat, floods and storms. The *right to food* is undermined by droughts and shifting weather. The *right to water* is squeezed by freshwater scarcity affecting billions. The *right to health* suffers as climate change spreads disease and pollution. The *right to housing* is destroyed when rising seas and disasters wipe out homes. And the *right to self-determination* faces an existential test for small island nations that may literally vanish beneath the waves.

This is where the idea of **climate justice** becomes important, and it is worth stating in a balanced way. The countries that have contributed the *least* to greenhouse gas emissions are often the *most* affected; wealthy nations have more resources to adapt, while poorer ones bear the brunt; future generations will inherit the consequences of today's choices; and indigenous and marginalised communities are hit hardest. In a landmark step, the UN General Assembly in 2022 recognised the right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment as a universal human right -- a significant move in linking environmental protection to human rights. A particularly thorny problem is the *rights gap* for people displaced by climate: someone forced from their home by drought or rising seas does not fit the legal definition of a "refugee," which covers persecution, so they fall through the cracks of international law -- a gap the framework has yet to close.

questions.task: Why is climate change considered a human rights issue?

options.text: Because it has no effect on people
Because it only affects wealthy nations
Because it is purely a scientific question
Because it threatens rights to life, food, water, health and housing

questions.solution: Climate change directly threatens fundamental rights to life, food, water, health, housing and even self-determination for some nations.

options.text: That those least responsible for emissions are often most affected
That all countries are affected equally
That only future generations are affected
That climate change benefits poorer nations

questions.solution: Climate justice highlights the inequity that the countries contributing least to emissions often suffer the most, while the wealthy can better afford to adapt.

questions.task: Why do people displaced by climate change fall into a "rights gap"?

options.text: Because they are wealthy
Because the legal definition of "refugee" covers persecution, not climate displacement
Because they choose not to claim rights
Because climate change does not cause displacement

questions.solution: International law defines refugees in terms of persecution, so people displaced by climate impacts are not covered, leaving a gap in legal protection.

questions.task: What did the UN General Assembly recognise as a universal human right in 2022?

options.text: The right to fossil fuels
The right to unlimited consumption
The right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment
The right to ignore the climate

questions.solution: In 2022 the UN General Assembly recognised the right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment as a universal human right.

content.content:
## The double-edged sword of technology

The other defining challenge is digital. The twenty-first century has seen the rise of **digital authoritarianism**, in which governments use technology to monitor, control and suppress their populations in ways that would once have been impossible. The tools include mass surveillance of communications and movements; facial recognition systems that track individuals in public; social credit systems that rate citizens' behaviour and reward or punish them, as in China; internet censorship that blocks websites and even shuts down access entirely; and spyware such as Pegasus, used to infiltrate the phones of journalists and activists. The human rights at stake are clear: the right to privacy, freedom of expression, freedom of association, and even the right to seek asylum when refugees are tracked. Freedom House reports that internet freedom has declined for over a decade, with authoritarian states growing more sophisticated and even exporting their surveillance technology abroad.

But here is the crucial balance, and it is worth holding onto. The very same technology that enables surveillance can also empower citizens. Social media, encrypted messaging and other digital tools help activists organise, communicate and hold governments to account. Technology is a double-edged sword -- it can tighten control or break it open, depending on who wields it and how. That ambiguity runs through all the challenges in this chapter. The rise of authoritarianism globally is rolling back democratic freedoms, and spyware aimed at journalists raises hard questions about the responsibility of the corporations that build these tools. The conclusion is not despair but adaptation: the human rights framework must evolve to address twenty-first-century dangers -- climate, surveillance, displacement, resurgent authoritarianism -- while holding firm to its core principles of universality and human dignity.

options.text: placeholder
The use of technology by citizens to organise protests
A type of social media platform
A human rights treaty

questions.solution: Digital authoritarianism is the use of technology -- surveillance, censorship, facial recognition -- by governments to monitor and suppress their populations.

questions.task: Why does the chapter describe technology as a "double-edged sword"?

options.text: Because the same tools can enable surveillance and also empower activists
Because it is only ever harmful
Because it has no effect on rights
Because only governments can use it

questions.solution: The same technology that enables surveillance can also help activists organise and hold governments accountable, making it double-edged.

questions.task: Which human right is most directly threatened by mass surveillance?

options.text: The right to a fair wage
The right to privacy
The right to leisure
The right to vote at 16

questions.solution: Mass surveillance most directly threatens the right to privacy, along with freedom of expression and association.

questions.task: What is the chapter's overall conclusion about the human rights framework?

options.text: It should be abandoned
It is already perfect and needs no change
It must evolve to meet new challenges while keeping its core principles
It applies only to the past

questions.solution: The chapter concludes the framework must adapt to 21st-century challenges while preserving its core principles of universality and dignity.

content.content:
## In short

The human rights framework, built after the Second World War, now faces challenges its authors never imagined. Climate change threatens rights to life, food, water, health and housing, with the poorest countries hit hardest -- the heart of climate justice -- and people displaced by climate fall into a legal rights gap. Digital authoritarianism uses surveillance, censorship, facial recognition and spyware to suppress populations, threatening privacy, expression and association, even as the same technologies can empower activists. Authoritarianism is resurgent worldwide. The lesson is that technology and global change are double-edged, and that the framework must evolve to meet new dangers while holding firm to its founding principles of universality and dignity.
